script.opening: "The back of my ankle’s been sore and stiff for a few weeks — worst first thing and when I start a run, then it eases a bit. There’s a tender, slightly swollen lump on the tendon. I’ve upped my running lately. What is it, and can I keep running?"

facts.text: Right Achilles, about 6 weeks, came on gradually. Stiff and sore for the first steps in the morning and the first 10 minutes of a run, eases, then aches afterwards and the next morning. A tender, thickened lump about 4 cm above the heel bone — points to it on camera.

No sudden "kick" or pop, no snap, never felt as if someone hit the back of his leg. Can still run. If asked to try on video: can do a single-leg tiptoe on the right, 10 times, though it’s sore. If his wife squeezes his calf while he kneels on a chair (if the doctor guides it): his foot moves down normally.
Training for a half-marathon: went from 15 km to 40 km a week over a month, added hill sprints, new lighter racing shoes.

No recent antibiotics (no ciprofloxacin or similar). No steroid tablets or injections. No other joints painful, no back stiffness, no psoriasis, no eye inflammation, no gout. Cholesterol never checked; no yellow lumps on tendons.
Fit. No medicines; occasional ibuprofen after runs. No allergies. Office manager. Married with two children. Non-smoker.

Keen runner, a little impatient. Main question: can you keep running? Relieved if told you can run at a lower level within a pain limit. Ask: "Could I just have a steroid injection to speed things up?" Accept when told why not.

ice.concerns: "Whether it could snap, and whether I have to stop running altogether — the half-marathon is in 8 weeks."
ice.expectations: "To keep running, and maybe an injection to speed it up."

checkpoints.text: Recognises ACHILLES TENDINOPATHY (gradual load-related posterior ankle pain, morning/start-of-activity stiffness, tender thickened tendon, training-load increase), distinguishing mid-portion from insertional disease
EXCLUDES acute ACHILLES RUPTURE (sudden pop, weakness, inability to tip-toe, palpable gap, positive Simmonds/Thompson test) — a must-not-miss needing same-day orthopaedic/fracture-clinic assessment

Considers the differential (gout, bursitis, spondyloarthritis enthesitis, xanthomata, referred pain) and reviews RISK factors — training load, fluoroquinolone antibiotics (tendinopathy/rupture; MHRA 2019 and January 2024), steroids
Manages conservatively with the cornerstone progressive LOADING (eccentric/heavy-slow) programme via physiotherapy, load modification (modify rather than stop), analgesia, footwear/heel raise

AVOIDS corticosteroid injection into the Achilles (rupture risk) and refers (physio/orthopaedics-sports medicine if refractory; urgently if rupture suspected), setting realistic (about three months) expectations
Addresses his wish to keep running, explains the diagnosis/timeline, and checks understanding of the rehab plan
Shares the decision about training load openly, agreeing what he will modify and a realistic timescale, so he feels in control rather than banned from running
Safety-nets and follows up: review if not improving/refractory, urgent assessment if rupture features develop, and risk-factor modification — loading rehab, not steroid injection

worked.txt: "This is Achilles tendinopathy — an overuse strain of the tendon, set off by upping your running. The stiffness worst first thing and at the start of a run, with that tender thickened spot, is classic."

"Let me make sure it isn’t a tear — did it ever suddenly pop, and can you push off and stand on tip-toes? … Yes. And the calf-squeeze test is normal. Good — a sudden rupture is the thing we never miss."

"Quick check — have you had a quinolone antibiotic like ciprofloxacin recently, or steroid tablets or injections? They can affect tendons, even months after stopping. And we’ll look at your training load, which is the main driver here."

"The treatment that genuinely works is a progressive strengthening programme — specific calf/tendon loading exercises — with physiotherapy. You don’t have to stop running completely; we modify the load rather than rest entirely — keep the pain mild during a run and make sure it has settled by the next morning."
"One thing I won’t do is inject steroid into the tendon — that raises the risk of it rupturing. The exercises are the way."

"Be patient — it usually takes about three months; let’s review at around 12 weeks, or sooner if it’s getting worse. If you ever feel a sudden pop and can’t push off or stand on tiptoe, go to A&E the same day — that would need same-day assessment."

f.learning: ACHILLES TENDINOPATHY is an overuse condition presenting with gradual-onset posterior ankle/heel pain and stiffness, worst on STARTING activity and in the MORNING, with localised tenderness and THICKENING of the tendon (mid-portion ~2–6 cm above the insertion, or insertional where the tendon meets the heel bone), typically provoked by training-load increases, poor footwear and calf tightness. The must-not-miss is ACUTE ACHILLES RUPTURE — a sudden "kicked/popped" sensation, weakness, inability to push off/stand on tip-toes, a palpable gap and a positive SIMMONDS/Thompson calf-squeeze test (no plantarflexion on squeezing the calf) — which is easily missed (some patients still weakly plantarflex) and needs same-day orthopaedic or fracture-clinic assessment. Consider gout, retrocalcaneal bursitis, spondyloarthritis enthesitis (NICE NG65), xanthomata and referred pain, and review risk factors including training-load spikes, FLUOROQUINOLONE antibiotics (ciprofloxacin — tendinopathy/rupture risk; MHRA Drug Safety Update March 2019, and since January 2024 only when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate), corticosteroids and inflammatory arthropathy, stopping/avoiding fluoroquinolones if implicated. Manage conservatively: relative rest/load modification (reduce running volume rather than stop entirely), analgesia, and the cornerstone — a structured progressive LOADING programme (eccentric/heavy-slow resistance) via physiotherapy with calf stretching and footwear/heel raise — which is evidence-based (JOSPT/APTA 2024, international) and effective but slow (about three months). AVOID corticosteroid injection into the Achilles tendon (rupture risk), refer to physiotherapy (and orthopaedics/sports medicine if refractory, urgently if rupture suspected), and set realistic expectations (review at around 12 weeks; shockwave only with special arrangements, NICE HTG426).

knowledge.summary: Gradual, load-related pain at the back of the heel, stiff first thing and at the start of exercise, with a tender thickened tendon after a jump in training, is Achilles tendinopathy. First make sure it is not a rupture: ask about a sudden pop, check he can stand on tiptoe and do the calf-squeeze test. Then treat with load modification and a progressive loading programme, usually through physiotherapy, and set expectations of about three months. Check for fluoroquinolone use. Do not inject steroid into the Achilles.

points.t: Pain and stiffness at the back of the heel that comes on gradually, is worst in the morning and at the start of activity, eases as he warms up and returns afterwards. Mid-portion disease gives a tender, thickened area a few centimetres above the heel bone; insertional disease is tender where the tendon meets the bone. A recent increase in training load is the usual trigger.

A sudden ‘kicked’ or ‘popped’ feeling, weakness pushing off, inability to do a single-leg tiptoe, a palpable gap and a positive calf-squeeze (Simmonds or Thompson) test point to rupture. The squeeze test is sensitive and specific (Maffulli 1998 [5]), but some people with a rupture can still point the foot using other muscles. Suspected rupture needs same-day orthopaedic or fracture-clinic assessment.

Retrocalcaneal bursitis, insertional disease with a bony prominence, gout, a spondyloarthritis enthesitis (NICE NG65 [6]), bilateral tendon thickening from xanthomata, and referred pain. Ask about fluoroquinolone antibiotics: tendon damage can start within 48 hours or months after stopping, and risk is higher over 60, with renal impairment and with a corticosteroid (MHRA [2]). Since January 2024 fluoroquinolones should only be used when other recommended antibiotics are inappropriate.

Tendon-loading exercise is the best-supported treatment (JOSPT/APTA 2024 [1]). Common programmes are eccentric heel drops or heavy slow resistance, progressed over about 12 weeks. He can keep running at a lower volume if pain stays at a tolerable level during activity and has settled by the next morning. Heel lifts and footwear changes are adjuncts.

Paracetamol or a topical NSAID can help pain; if an oral NSAID is used, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (BNF; MHRA June 2015 [7]). Doses as per BNF. Analgesia does not treat the tendon and should not be used to run through pain.

Do not inject corticosteroid into the Achilles tendon: the product literature states it should not be injected because of rupture risk [3]. Shockwave therapy is available only with special arrangements for governance and consent (NICE HTG426 [4]).

Review at around 12 weeks. Refer to physiotherapy early, and to sports medicine or orthopaedics if there is no improvement after about three months of good adherence, if the diagnosis is uncertain, or urgently if rupture is suspected.

model.text: Hello Mr Easton, I’m Dr Shah. What can I help with today?

The back of my ankle’s been sore and stiff for a few weeks. It’s worst first thing and when I start a run, then it eases a bit. There’s a tender, slightly swollen lump on the tendon. I’ve upped my running lately. What is it, and can I keep running?
So two questions: what it is, and whether you can keep running. I’d like to ask a few things, look at the ankle on the camera, and then answer both properly. Is that alright?
model.why: Summarises his two questions and sets the agenda

model.text: Yes, that’s exactly what I want to know.
How did it start? Was it gradual, or was there a moment when something went?
Gradual. It just crept up over a few weeks.
Have you ever felt a sudden kick or pop at the back of the ankle, as if someone hit you, or found you couldn’t push off?
No, nothing like that. I can still run, it just hurts.
Tell me about the running. What changed?
I’ve been building up the distance quite quickly, a few more runs a week.
Where exactly is the pain: a few centimetres up the tendon, or right where it joins the heel bone? And is it one side only?
Just this side, and a bit up from the heel, where the lump is.
Have you had any antibiotics recently, especially one called ciprofloxacin or a similar one, or any steroid tablets or injections?
No, nothing like that.
Any pain or swelling in other joints, back stiffness in the mornings, eye or skin problems, or a hot, red joint like gout?
No, it’s just this.
How is it affecting you day to day, at work and outside running?
It’s mainly the running. I really don’t want to stop.
What do you think is going on?
I assume I’ve strained the tendon from running more.
Is anything in particular worrying you?
Whether it could snap, and whether I have to stop running altogether.

Could you show me both ankles on the camera, run your fingers along the tendon and tell me if you feel a lump or a gap, then go up on tiptoe on each leg? If someone is with you, I’ll talk them through squeezing your calf while you kneel on a chair, to check the tendon is intact.
model.why: Targeted video examination including single-leg tiptoe and assisted calf-squeeze

model.text: Okay.

This fits Achilles tendinopathy. It’s an overload problem: the tendon has been asked to do more than it was ready for, so it has become painful and thickened. It isn’t a tear. You’re right to ask about snapping. A sudden pop with weakness is the thing I never want to miss, and that isn’t your story.
model.why: Names the diagnosis and addresses the rupture fear

model.text: That’s a relief. So what do I do?

The treatment that works best is specific strengthening exercises for the calf and tendon, built up gradually over about three months. I’ll refer you to physiotherapy to set that up. You don’t need to stop running completely. Would you be willing to cut the distance for now and keep the pain during a run mild, as long as it has settled by the next morning?
model.why: Loading programme, physiotherapy and load modification shared as a choice

model.text: Yes, I can do shorter, easier runs if it means I keep going.

Good. For pain, paracetamol or an anti-inflammatory gel can help. They take the edge off but they don’t heal the tendon, so don’t use them to run through pain. A small heel raise in your shoe can ease it in the meantime.
Could I just have a steroid injection to speed things up?

I wouldn’t inject steroid into this tendon. It can weaken it and make a rupture more likely. The exercises are the way to get it stronger. If you ever need an antibiotic, tell the prescriber about this tendon problem, because one group of antibiotics can affect tendons.
model.why: Declines steroid injection with a reason; future fluoroquinolone caution

model.text: Fair enough.

If you ever feel a sudden pop or kick at the back of the ankle and can’t push off or stand on tiptoe, go to A&E the same day, because a rupture needs treating quickly. Otherwise let’s review in about 12 weeks, or sooner if it’s getting worse despite the changes. What will you do between now and then?
model.why: Rupture safety net, follow-up and teach-back

model.text: Shorter runs keeping the pain mild, the physio exercises every day, gel if I need it, no injection. A&E if it pops.
Exactly right. It’s slow but it does get better with the exercises.

social.t: Running matters to him. A plan that keeps him active supports his wellbeing and his engagement with treatment.
Most people with tendinopathy can work normally. If a job involves a lot of standing or walking, discuss adjustments or a fit note only if needed.

legal.t: Record the tendinopathy, so any future fluoroquinolone prescription takes the MHRA warning into account (Drug Safety Update March 2019 and January 2024). Report suspected tendon reactions through the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: Declining a requested injection with a clear reason, and offering an effective alternative, respects his autonomy while keeping to safe practice (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Local MSK physiotherapy (self-referral where available) and graded return-to-run plans through running clubs or community programmes.

redFlags: Sudden pop or kick with weakness: suspected rupture, same-day assessment
Unable to do a single-leg tiptoe or positive calf-squeeze test
Hot, swollen joint or features of inflammatory arthritis
psychosocial: Running matters a lot to him
Fear of having to stop running
ice: Concern: rupture; having to stop running
Expectation: a diagnosis and permission to keep running

playbook.diagnosis: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy after a rapid increase in running load; rupture excluded clinically.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The tendon has been overloaded by the extra running, so it has become sore and thickened. It isn’t torn. It gets better by gradually making it stronger.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried it might snap and that you’d have to stop running. It isn’t torn, and you can keep running at a lower level.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him active; agree a pain rule he can use himself.
sharedPlan: Physiotherapy referral for a progressive loading programme over about 12 weeks
Reduce running volume; pain mild during runs and settled by next morning
Paracetamol or topical NSAID; heel raise
No corticosteroid injection; caution with future fluoroquinolones
safetyNet: Sudden pop, weakness or unable to tiptoe: A&E the same day
Review at about 12 weeks; refer on if not improving

pitfalls.intro: This is an easy diagnosis. The marks are for excluding rupture, giving the treatment that works and keeping a keen runner on side.

items.why: A missed rupture has a worse outcome if treatment is delayed.
items.fix: Ask about a pop, test single-leg tiptoe and do the calf-squeeze test.

items.why: Loading exercise is the evidence-based treatment.
items.fix: Refer for a progressive loading programme and modify, not stop, running.
Ask, and flag the risk for future prescribing.

items.why: He will likely ignore it and disengage.
items.fix: Agree a pain rule and reduced volume together.

items.why: He may give up early or miss a rupture.
items.fix: About three months; A&E for a sudden pop; review at 12 weeks.

wordPics.fail: Tells him to stop running and rest, or offers a steroid injection; does not check for rupture; no timescale.
wordPics.pass: Diagnoses tendinopathy, excludes rupture, starts a loading programme with physiotherapy and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: agrees a pain rule so he can keep running, explains why the injection is avoided, asks about fluoroquinolones, sets a realistic three-month timeline and checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “You need to stop running until it’s better.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s cut the distance and keep the pain mild while the exercises strengthen the tendon.”
avoid.why: Complete rest deconditions the tendon; load modification keeps him engaged.

avoid.dont: “A steroid injection will settle it quickly.”
avoid.instead: “I won’t inject this tendon, because it can weaken it and make a tear more likely.”
avoid.why: Corticosteroid should not be injected into the Achilles tendon (SPC).

avoid.dont: “It’ll be better in a couple of weeks.”
avoid.instead: “It usually takes around three months of exercises.”
avoid.why: False timescales lead to frustration and early return to full load.

Paracetamol or a topical NSAID can help pain; if an oral NSAID is used, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time (BNF; MHRA June 2015 [7]). Doses as per BNF. Analgesia does not treat the tendon and should not be used to run through pain.

Do not inject corticosteroid into the Achilles tendon: the product literature states it should not be injected because of rupture risk [3]. Shockwave therapy is available only with special arrangements for governance and consent (NICE HTG426 [4]).

Review at around 12 weeks. Refer to physiotherapy early, and to sports medicine or orthopaedics if there is no improvement after about three months of good adherence, if the diagnosis is uncertain, or urgently if rupture is suspected.

social.t: Running matters to him. A plan that keeps him active supports his wellbeing and his engagement with treatment.
Most people with tendinopathy can work normally. If a job involves a lot of standing or walking, discuss adjustments or a fit note only if needed.

legal.t: Record the tendinopathy, so any future fluoroquinolone prescription takes the MHRA warning into account (Drug Safety Update March 2019 and January 2024). Report suspected tendon reactions through the Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: Declining a requested injection with a clear reason, and offering an effective alternative, respects his autonomy while keeping to safe practice (GMC Good medical practice).

community.t: Local MSK physiotherapy (self-referral where available) and graded return-to-run plans through running clubs or community programmes.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy after a rapid increase in running load; rupture excluded clinically.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The tendon has been overloaded by the extra running, so it has become sore and thickened. It isn’t torn. It gets better by gradually making it stronger.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried it might snap and that you’d have to stop running. It isn’t torn, and you can keep running at a lower level.”

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is an easy diagnosis. The marks are for excluding rupture, giving the treatment that works and keeping a keen runner on side.

items.why: A missed rupture has a worse outcome if treatment is delayed.
items.fix: Ask about a pop, test single-leg tiptoe and do the calf-squeeze test.

items.why: Loading exercise is the evidence-based treatment.
items.fix: Refer for a progressive loading programme and modify, not stop, running.
Ask, and flag the risk for future prescribing.

items.fix: Agree a pain rule and reduced volume together.
